results.summary: This project is a silicon design evolution experiment that gradually modifies the Tiny Tapeout template to perform more tasks. It uses an 8-bit input bus and an 8-bit output bus, with no external hardware required. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it is a gradual evolution and that testing methods are yet to be determined. There is no clear description of the specific functions or tasks implemented.

This design implements a bytebeat formula in hardware, generating 8-bit PCM audio samples from four 4-bit parameters. It accepts parameters via input and bidirectional pins and outputs the PCM sample on the output pins. The design is written in XLS and can be easily modified to change the formula. It requires an external 8-bit parallel DAC to convert the digital samples to analog audio.

This project is a compilation of bytebeat formulas that generate PWM audio signals on multiple output pins. It takes four 4-bit parameters and produces different bytebeat tunes on pins 0, 3, and 7, with other pins unused. The design is written in XLS and can be regenerated with modified formulas. It requires external rotary switches for parameter adjustment and speakers or a TinyTapeout Audio PMOD to hear the output.

This design uses two buttons to adjust the brightness of an LED dot on a 7-segment display. The current brightness level is shown as a number on the display. It requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout board's built-in buttons and display. The project is a simple demonstration of PWM-based LED dimming with user input.

This is a simple 8-bit CPU inspired by Ben Eater's design and the game Turing Complete, created in a four-hour sprint before the submission deadline. It has an 8-bit input bus and an 8-bit output bus, with no bidirectional pins used. Testing requires an RP2040 or RP2350 on a test board acting as a memory controller to run programs. The documentation is sparse and does not detail the instruction set or architecture.

This is a calculator that accepts two 4-bit operands and an operation (addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division) via input pins, and outputs an 8-bit result. A strobe signal indicates when a button is pressed. Division rounds upwards, and zero is not supported as an operand. It requires an external hexadecimal keypad for input and displays to show the result.

This design is a two-channel RC servo pulse generator that produces standard 20 ms PWM frames with pulse widths between 1.0 ms and 2.0 ms based on two asynchronous comparator inputs. It uses a 50 MHz clock and has active-low reset and enable signals. The outputs are PWM signals for X and Y axes. Testing involves driving the comparator inputs with digital levels and observing the PWM outputs on a scope or in simulation.

This project is a simple reaction test game implemented in VHDL. It has one input pin and one output pin, but the documentation does not describe how the game works or how to interact with it. The description states only that it works and to send in data. There is no information on external hardware or testing procedures.

This design displays animated arrow signs for traffic control using 25 LEDs arranged in a specific pattern. It supports 16 selectable patterns with options for flashing and sequential animation, controlled by input pins. The outputs drive the LEDs directly, and the design includes a lamp test and active-low control. It requires an external array of 25 LEDs connected to the output and bidirectional pins.

This is a modified FemtoRV RISC-V SoC that uses a register file from tnt and a QSPI controller from TinyQV. It executes code from QSPI flash and uses QSPI PSRAM for data memory, with shared clock and data lines. The SoC includes a UART and an SPI controller, and is intended to work with a QSPI PMOD containing flash and RAM, as well as an ST7789 LCD display. Silicon testing showed it works perfectly, even at 80 MHz, and a minimal MicroPython binary was run on it.
